subject: Medicine
summary: Gout is an acute inflammatory arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints, triggered by hyperuricemia. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, crystal identification, and serum urate levels. Management balances acute control with long‑term urate lowering.

sections.p: Gout is the deposition of needle‑shaped monosodium urate crystals in and around joints, producing sudden, intense pain and swelling. Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying negatively birefringent crystals on polarized microscopy of synovial fluid or by clinical criteria plus serum urate >6.8 mg/dL.

t.b: Does the joint fluid contain needle‑shaped, negatively birefringent crystals? A positive result confirms gout.
Is urate >6.8 mg/dL? Elevated levels support the diagnosis but are not definitive alone.
Shows joint erosions or tophi in chronic disease; normal in acute attacks.

sections.p: Acute gout is staged by attack frequency and chronicity. The 2016 ACR/EULAR classification uses acute attacks, tophi, and radiographic damage to define stages I–IV.
b: Stage I: single attack, no tophi
Stage II: recurrent attacks, no tophi
Stage III: tophi present, no erosions
Stage IV: erosions or joint damage

sections.p: Hyperuricemia results from overproduction, underexcretion, or both. Common precipitating factors include high purine diet, alcohol, diuretics, obesity, and renal impairment.
b: Overproduction: high purine intake, cell turnover
Underexcretion: renal disease, diuretics, low salt intake

t.b: Is renal function impaired? Reduced excretion increases urate.
Low urine urate suggests underexcretion; high suggests overproduction.

sections.p: Typical presentation is sudden, severe pain in the first MTP joint (podagra), with erythema, warmth, and limited motion. Attacks last 24–48 h and may recur.
Key tests confirm diagnosis and guide management. In low‑resource settings, basic labs and clinical criteria are often sufficient.

t.b: Positive = gout; negative = consider pseudogout or other arthritides.
>6.8 mg/dL supports diagnosis but not definitive.
Elevated values may indicate infection or systemic disease.
Impaired function may alter choice of urate‑lowering drugs.

sections.p: Severe or recurrent attacks can lead to tophi, joint destruction, renal stones, and chronic kidney disease. Urgent care is needed for signs of infection or systemic involvement.
Treat the acute attack first, then initiate long‑term urate lowering. Choice of drugs depends on renal function, comorbidities, and drug availability.
b: Long‑term: xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol, febuxostat) or uricosurics (probenecid)

t.b: Avoid in renal impairment or GI ulcer risk.
Toxicity in renal failure; dose adjustment needed.
Start low, titrate; avoid in severe renal disease without dose adjustment.
Monitor liver function; avoid in severe hepatic disease.
Contraindicated in renal impairment or urinary stones.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of serum urate, renal function, and adherence is essential. Lifestyle changes reduce recurrence.
Pseudogout, septic arthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis can mimic gout but differ in crystal type and clinical course.
b: Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetric polyarthritis, morning stiffness

sections.p: Serum urate can be normal during an acute attack; crystal analysis is definitive. Renal function tests may be falsely normal early in kidney disease.
b: Early renal impairment may not raise creatinine yet

faq.a: There is no cure, but long‑term urate lowering can prevent attacks and joint damage.

faq.q: Why is serum urate sometimes normal in gout?
faq.a: During an acute flare, urate may be consumed by crystals, lowering serum levels.
Yes, alcohol increases urate production and reduces excretion, precipitating attacks.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of monosodium urate crystal formation and its clinical consequences.
Describe the diagnostic criteria for gout and the role of synovial fluid analysis.
Outline the first‑line acute treatment and the rationale for long‑term urate‑lowering therapy.
